fields.meta_title: Telemedicine Consent Form for Virtual Visits | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a telemedicine consent form that logs verbal or signed consent, names everyone on the call, and asks where the patient is today.
fields.h1: Build a Telemedicine Consent Form for Video and Phone Visits
fields.hero_description: Get a telemedicine consent form that saves each patient's e-signature or spoken yes, plus a callback number for every visit.
fields.features_heading: Consent That Follows the Patient Into the Visit
fields.features_subheading: Every answer saves to a database you own, and the app can email the front desk when tomorrow's patient has not agreed yet.
fields.feature_1:
A link that goes out with the booking

The consent link rides along with the appointment confirmation. AHRQ advises sending the form in advance so patients can review it ahead of time, then e-sign on a phone.
fields.feature_2:
A verbal yes, with the staff member's name

Some patients never open a link. Staff mark Verbal consent given at check-in, and the app stamps the record with the staff member's name and the exact minute it happened.
fields.feature_3:
Everyone on the call, listed and approved

A caregiver, an interpreter, or a student clinician gets a line of their own. The patient approves each name before the visit starts, and the record keeps who was there.
fields.feature_4:
Where the patient is today

HHS guidance says to confirm the patient's exact location at the beginning of each telemedicine appointment. Check-in asks for that address and a number to call back.
fields.feature_5:
Video, phone, or either

Patients pick the visit types they accept right on the form. The choice is saved next to their consent, so the scheduling screen can read it before anyone books a slot.
fields.feature_6:
A teach-back checklist for staff

AHRQ recommends teach-back to confirm patients understand. Staff get a short list of topics with a yes or no beside each: did the patient explain it in their own words?
fields.why_title: Why Build Telemedicine Consent on Emergent?
fields.why_description: A consent PDF ends at the signature line. Emergent builds the check-in steps a video visit needs too, from one prompt.

fields.usecase_heading: What Happens Between Check-In and the Doctor
fields.tab_content_1:
When the patient has no portal, Noor reads it aloud

Desmond Achterberg has no portal login at Harlow Bend Family Practice. At 9:04 AM, medical assistant Noor Abernethy reads him the consent summary over video and he agrees out loud. She ticks Verbal consent given, and her name and the time save to his record before Dr. Sabine Oyelaran joins.
fields.tab_content_2:
Arturo said yes before Lucia joined the call

Sorrel Creek Geriatrics adds a line to check-in for anyone else on the call. Lucia Ferreira is joining her father Arturo's video visit, so the screen lists her as a participant, and Arturo's yes to having her there saves before the doctor starts.
fields.tab_content_3:
Video froze at 3:22 and the callback number was there

Every session at Wrenfield Counseling opens with two questions for the client: the street address they are at right now, and a number to call back. When Tobias Lindqvist's video freezes at 3:22 PM, therapist Mireille Okonjo calls him on that number and finishes the session by phone.
fields.tab_content_4:
For Harriet, a phone slot instead of video

Harriet Kowalczyk ticked phone visits only on her consent at Thistledown Health. When Gideon Mbatha at the front desk tries to book her follow-up as a video visit, the scheduling screen blocks it and offers a phone slot at 2:30 PM Thursday instead.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is nine clinic PDFs: a page of I-understand clauses and one signature line, signed once and filed. None of them handles what happens around a video visit: a patient with no portal who agrees out loud, a family member who joins the call, a video that freezes mid-session, or a patient who agreed to phone visits only. This page builds those moments into the form, using only what HHS and AHRQ publish about telehealth consent (with their limits: rules vary by state, wording goes to the practice's legal team) and never says the form makes consent valid.
